intro_en: The Israel National Trail leaves the tourist hotel district – and turns back toward the desert landscapes. In the first part of the day we walk as far as Nahal Ashalim, through a landscape of cliffs, acacia trees and hard rock. After crossing the channel of Nahal Ashalim, the scenery changes to pale, dissected marl hills with a view toward the salt mountain – Mount Sodom.
character_en: (For those walking north to south) We walk in Nahal Rom and Nahal Zohar on a slightly challenging route with ascents and descents among rocks and high rock steps. Most of the route is exposed to the sun, with short shaded sections in Nahal Rom, the Zohar canyon and Nahal Peratzim.
description_en:
We start walking in the tourist area with its Dead Sea hotels, shops and malls. Beside them, on the shore of the evaporation ponds, are several regulated bathing beaches with the option of a dip for those who wish.
The trail proceeds along the sidewalk at the edge of the main road that crosses the hotel area from north to south. After a short walk, we cross on a bridge over the channel of Nahal Bokek; upstream lies the Ein Bokek spring.
We continue walking south, and on leaving the hotel area the trail climbs with the sidewalk beside the road to a higher level. The road crosses a bridge over Nahal Rom, and immediately at the southern exit from the bridge the trail turns right, climbs a low hill and descends its other side into the channel of Nahal Rom.
In an instant the tourist landscape gives way to a desert landscape – acacia trees and a desert streambed. The trail continues along the streambed, and a black marking accompanies the Israel National Trail marking up to the crossing of Road 90 – where it passes beneath the road through a tall culvert.
We climb up the channel of Nahal Rom, which cuts into the hard rock typical of the Judean Desert. We climb and hop between rocks and small dry waterfalls, up to the highest point of the segment – the watershed between Nahal Rom and Nahal Yizrah.
From here we can see the channel of Nahal Yizrah descending southward – an unusual flow direction for Judean Desert streams, which mostly flow from the mountain ridge down to the Dead Sea rift, from west to east. It was the north–south line of a geological fault that determined the course of Nahal Yizrah.
The trail descends into the channel of Nahal Yizrah, and acacia trees scattered along the streambed offer a shaded spot to stop and rest. During the descent along the channel, from a certain point on, soft white rocks appear – Lisan marl. These rocks are evidence of a "fjord" that penetrated the Nahal Yizrah channel in the geological past.
In Lake Lisan, the ancient ancestor of the Dead Sea, whose level stood high above the streambed, sediments were deposited that formed the Lisan marl rocks, named after the ancient lake.
In the final section of the stream, on the right bank, you can see a cave formed within the Lisan marl that has earned the nickname "the Elephant's Foot".
After a further short walk, the channel of Nahal Yizrah joins the channel of Nahal Zohar. It is recommended to turn right and climb for a 10–15 minute walk up the Nahal Zohar channel to reach Metzad Zohar – the remains of an ancient fort that controlled the Zohar ascent. The fort was built on a pale hill of Lisan marl.
The marking that accompanies the Israel National Trail marking changes from black to green. After crossing a blue-marked dirt road, we reach the lower part of Nahal Zohar.
The stream cuts and winds between limestone and conglomerate rocks (a rock formed from rounded rock fragments that joined together and hardened into a single rock) – through a beautiful canyon with two low dry waterfalls, which the trail shows us how to descend.
Toward the exit from the canyon, we pass beneath a high bridge – the Road 90 bridge over Nahal Zohar. A short distance from the bridge, on leaving the canyon, the trail exits the channel southward onto a dirt road and climbs toward a pumping facility. On the northern side of Nahal Zohar you can see the community of Neve Zohar.
We continue south with the dirt road, and cross Road 90 onto a blue-marked dirt road that leads to the channel of Nahal Hemar. Here you can walk a little east along the road to the gas station, to "refuel" with water and snacks.
From the channel we continue south-east with the green marking, and a little after passing the Nahal Lot overnight campsite, the Israel National Trail moves onto a red-marked track. In front of us rises a mountain of salt – none other than Mount Sodom.
We enter the channel of Nahal Peratzim and walk along the streambed between white walls etched with lines. Water and the forces of erosion sculpt the soft Lisan marl rock into shapes of pillars and palaces, creating a landscape unlike any other.
When the dirt road is blocked and the trail continues as a footpath, we pass the Flour Cave, which it is forbidden to enter because of collapses. The trail climbs out of the channel onto the Amiaz Plain. Then a broad plain is revealed – a wide plateau between the cliff to the west and Mount Sodom to the east. A short further walk south on the red-marked track brings us to the Amiaz Plain overnight campsite – the end of the segment.
nearby_en: Ein Bokek – Nahal Bokek, a short route with flowing water, free of charge.
The Mount Sodom lookout and the special trails that cross it.
Points of interest: Nahal Rom – Nahal Yizrah. The Nahal Zohar canyon. Metzad Zohar (a short distance from the trail). Nahal Peratzim. View toward Mount Sodom.
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, trail-marking coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
